concepts.name: Constitutional Basis and Status of the Election Commission
key_dimensions: Article 324: Exact text and scope — 'superintendence, direction and control' vs mere administration
Whether ECI is a constitutional body vs statutory body — distinction and implications
Comparison with bodies like CAG (Art 148), UPSC (Art 315) — similarities and differences in constitutional protection
Why ECI is NOT a quasi-judicial body in the traditional sense, yet exercises quasi-judicial functions

concepts.name: Composition of the Election Commission: Evolution from Single to Multi-Member Body
key_dimensions: Original Art 324 position: President's discretion to appoint one or more Election Commissioners
Historical shift — single-member ECI (1950–1989) to multi-member post 1989 via Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners Act
Current composition: CEC + 2 ECs — constitutional vs statutory basis of this number
UPSC trap: Constitution does NOT fix the number of members — it is left to Parliament/President

concepts.name: Appointment of CEC and Election Commissioners: Pre and Post 2023 Reform
key_dimensions: Pre-2023: President appointed CEC/ECs on advice of Council of Ministers — no statutory selection committee
Anoop Baranwal v. Union of India (2023 SC judgment): SC mandated a committee (PM + LoP + CJI) until Parliament legislates
Chief Election Commissioner and Other Election Commissioners (Appointment, Conditions of Service and Term of Office) Act, 2023 — replaced CJI with Cabinet Minister
Controversy: Whether exclusion of CJI undermines independence; comparison with collegium-style appointments

concepts.name: Security of Tenure: CEC vs Election Commissioners — The Asymmetry
key_dimensions: CEC: Removal only like a Supreme Court judge (Art 324(5)) — address of both Houses + special majority
ECs: Can be removed on recommendation of CEC — significantly weaker protection
UPSC trap: ECs do NOT enjoy the same constitutional removal protection as CEC
T.N. Seshan era controversy — attempted removal of ECs as a pressure tactic
2023 Act: Whether it equalised removal protection — still a debated area

concepts.name: Term of Office and Eligibility Conditions
key_dimensions: Six-year term OR 65 years of age, whichever is earlier — unlike judges who serve till age limit only
Not eligible for further appointment by the Government after retirement — constitutional bar under Art 324(5)
Salary and service conditions: Charged on Consolidated Fund of India (CEC) — insulating from budget vote
UPSC trap: Salary of ECs (not CEC) was earlier equivalent to SC judge but governed by statute, not Constitution directly

concepts.name: Superintendence, Direction and Control — Scope and Judicial Interpretation
key_dimensions: Art 324(1): Plenary and residuary power — ECI can fill gaps where law is silent (Mohinder Singh Gill v. CEC, 1978)
'Superintendence' implies supervisory + revisory authority over entire election machinery
ECI's power to issue Model Code of Conduct — not backed by any statute, derives from Art 324 alone
Limit: ECI cannot override explicit statutory provisions (Representation of People Act, 1950 & 1951)

concepts.name: Elections Covered by the Election Commission vs State Election Commissions
key_dimensions: ECI jurisdiction: Parliament, State Legislatures, President, Vice-President (Art 324)
State Election Commissions (Art 243K): Panchayats and Municipalities — entirely separate constitutional body
UPSC trap: ECI has NO role in Panchayat/Municipal elections — a frequent confusion point
Comparison: SEC under Art 243K vs ECI under Art 324 — appointment, removal, and independence levels

concepts.name: Model Code of Conduct: Legal Basis, Binding Nature and Limitations
key_dimensions: No statutory backing — purely derived from Art 324 and voluntary compliance tradition
Comes into force from date of announcement of election schedule, not notification of elections
MCC is NOT enforceable in courts as law — ECI enforces it through moral/political pressure and Art 324 powers
Controversy: Whether MCC should be given statutory backing — arguments for and against

concepts.name: Recognition of Political Parties and Allotment of Symbols
key_dimensions: Governed by Election Symbols (Reservation and Allotment) Order, 1968 — a statutory instrument under RPA
National Party vs State Party criteria — vote share % and seat thresholds (recently revised in 2023)
ECI's quasi-judicial role in disputes within parties (splits, mergers) — e.g., Shiv Sena and NCP 2023 rulings
UPSC trap: Symbol allotment is statutory power, not directly under Art 324 — RPA and Symbols Order govern it

concepts.name: Election Schedule and Enforcement: Powers During Election Period
key_dimensions: Power to postpone/advance elections — ECI can suspend/countermand elections on grounds of booth capturing, violence
Transfer and posting of election officials — ECI can override state government decisions during elections
Power to recommend imposition of President's Rule if free and fair elections are impossible? — controversial; not explicitly granted
Relationship between ECI orders and executive compliance — ECI has no enforcement machinery of its own

concepts.name: Delimitation Commission vs Election Commission — Overlapping but Distinct Functions
key_dimensions: Delimitation Commission: Statutory body under Delimitation Act, 2002 — draws constituency boundaries
ECI has NO role in delimitation — a common UPSC confusion point
However, ECI prepares electoral rolls (voters list) which is separate from delimitation
Delimitation Commission's orders are final and cannot be challenged in any court — unique feature

concepts.name: Electoral Rolls: Preparation, Revision and Controversies
key_dimensions: Governed by Representation of the People Act, 1950 — ECI supervises, EROs (Electoral Registration Officers) execute
Qualifying date for registration — currently 1st January; proposal to have 4 qualifying dates per year (2021 amendment)
Overseas voters and NRI voting rights — registered but cannot vote remotely; must appear in person
UPSC trap: Electoral roll preparation is ECI's function but voter ID (EPIC) is distinct from electoral registration

concepts.name: Disqualification of Candidates and Members: ECI's Role vs President/Governor
key_dimensions: Disqualification under Art 102/191 (general grounds) — decided by President/Governor on ECI's binding opinion (Art 103/192)
UPSC trap: President/Governor is bound by ECI opinion — they cannot act against it (not merely advisory)
Disqualification under Tenth Schedule (anti-defection) — decided by Speaker/Chairman, NOT ECI
Disqualification under RPA 1951 (corrupt practices, conviction) — decided by courts, ECI only receives reports

concepts.name: Election Commission's Powers on Corrupt Practices and Electoral Offences
key_dimensions: ECI cannot directly punish corrupt practices — these are tried by Election Tribunals/High Courts under RPA 1951
ECI CAN derecognize parties, cancel nominations, and refer matters under IPC for paid news, booth capturing
Power to order repoll — available under Sec 58A of RPA 1951 for booth capturing
Distinction: Electoral offence (criminal, court jurisdiction) vs corrupt practice (civil, election petition jurisdiction)

concepts.name: Expenditure Limits, Campaign Finance and ECI's Oversight Role
key_dimensions: Expenditure limits set by ECI under RPA 1951 — currently Rs 95 lakh for LS, Rs 40 lakh for assembly (revised 2022)
ECI appoints expenditure observers — powers to seize cash during elections
Electoral Bonds Scheme: SC struck down in ADR v. Union of India (2024) — ECI was a key petitioner-side witness
UPSC trap: ECI monitors candidate expenditure, NOT party expenditure — party limits are set separately under law

concepts.name: Judicial Review of Election Commission Decisions
key_dimensions: Art 329(b): Election disputes can only be raised through election petitions AFTER election, not during — major restriction on courts
Art 329(a): Validity of delimitation laws cannot be questioned in courts
However, ECI's administrative orders (not election itself) can be challenged under Art 226/32 — Mohinder Singh Gill principle
UPSC trap: Courts cannot interfere mid-election but CAN review ECI's non-election administrative actions

concepts.name: Electronic Voting Machines (EVMs) and VVPAT: ECI's Technological and Regulatory Role
key_dimensions: EVMs introduced nationally in 2004 — ECI adopted them using powers under Art 324 and RPA
VVPAT mandated after PUCL v. Union of India (2013) — SC directed paper trail
Recent controversy: 100% VVPAT counting demand — SC rejected in Association for Democratic Reforms (2024)
ECI as sole custodian of EVM technology — no private party involvement, manufactured by BEL and ECIL only

concepts.name: ECI and Media Regulation During Elections
key_dimensions: Power to enforce silence period — 48 hours before polling, no campaigning or exit polls
Exit poll restrictions: Under Sec 126A of RPA 1951 — ECI enforces, not creates this rule
Paid news: ECI can declare it as additional election expenditure — quasi-judicial function
Social media regulation during elections — ECI's Voluntary Code with platforms vs need for statutory backing

concepts.name: Independence of Election Commission: Structural Safeguards and Their Adequacy
key_dimensions: Safeguards: Security of tenure (CEC), charged expenditure, post-retirement bar on government appointment
Weaknesses: ECs lack same removal protection as CEC; appointment still executive-dominated post-2023 Act
Comparison with independent election bodies globally — Australia (AEC), UK (Electoral Commission) — multi-party appointment
Debate: Whether ECI needs a dedicated secretariat independent of government for staffing — current dependence on IAS officers

concepts.name: Election Commission and Bye-Elections, Mid-Term Polls and Simultaneous Elections
key_dimensions: Bye-election must be held within 6 months of vacancy — statutory obligation under RPA, ECI schedules it
Exception: If remainder of term is less than 1 year OR ECI certifies it is not reasonably practicable
Simultaneous elections ('One Nation One Vote') — requires constitutional amendments; ECI has supported in principle
UPSC trap: ECI cannot unilaterally decide to hold simultaneous elections — requires changes to Arts 83, 85, 172, 174, 356
